I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

I have to be on guard all the time
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: For a 55-year-old female bank teller with combat trauma, 'Bicycle' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items imply interpersonal/loss and sensory trauma reminders, while bicycle is a highly specific cue with no support from threat, memory, or appraisal content and no clear combat linkage. This makes it clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' is too nonspecific relative to the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize overt vigilance and reading faces/body language, and the appraisals also center betrayal and loss of meaning. This item implies diffuse interpersonal mistrust without a corresponding interpersonal memory or trigger pattern beyond betrayal, making the negative appraisal set less coherent with the otherwise combat/loss-focused formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around combat-linked threat, sensory triggers, and disjointed trauma memory, but the betrayal appraisal introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme that is not supported by the other selected items. With combat trauma, betrayal can occur, but here there are no corresponding triggers, memory content, or threat/appraisal items suggesting moral injury, friendly-fire, command betrayal, or interpersonal violation. This makes the betrayal item the main clinically incoherent element relative to the rest of the profile and formulation.

vignette: Maria, a 55-year-old Latin American woman who worked as a bank teller in her community, had experienced significant trauma during her time serving in combat. The event that still haunts her was a sudden explosion that killed several of her fellow soldiers and left Maria with severe physical and emotional scars. Maria’s life has been profoundly affected by the traumatic memories she carries. Whenever she hears loud noises or feels certain textures—specifically, the rough fabric of her old uniform—she is immediately transported back to the moment of the explosion. These triggers are so potent that they trigger intense physical reactions: her heart races, and she finds herself sweating profusely as if she were reliving the event in real time. The auditory stimuli, particularly loud bangs or explosions, can instantly send Maria into a state of hypervigilance. She begins to study people's faces and body language intensely, always looking for signs that they might be a threat. This hyperalertness is constant; she scans her surroundings almost obsessively, unable to relax even in familiar settings like the bank where she works. The memory itself feels surreal to Maria. When she tries to recount what happened during the explosion, she often loses track of her story and cannot put events into the correct sequence. The extremity of the event makes it difficult for her to believe that it truly occurred, yet the emotional intensity is undeniable. These fragmented memories frequently surface in her daily life, triggered by sounds or textures that remind her of combat. The constant triggers not only heighten Maria’s sense of threat but also exacerbate her negative appraisals about the world and her place within it. She has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place and that she must be on guard all the time. This hypervigilance has taken its toll on her daily functioning, particularly at work. Her constant scanning for danger makes it difficult to focus on her tasks as a bank teller, leading to mistakes and increased stress. Maria’s negative appraisals extend beyond just feeling threatened; she also feels that nothing in her life has any meaning anymore. The traumatic event seems to have stripped away much of the purpose she once found in daily activities. Her hypervigilance further reinforces these feelings, as she perceives danger around every corner and begins to isolate herself from others. For instance, at work, a sudden explosion-like sound during a bank transaction can trigger a full-blown panic attack. Maria feels her heart racing and starts sweating profusely. She scans the faces of customers, looking for any signs of threat, which often causes them discomfort and disrupts their transactions. This has led to an increase in customer complaints and strained relationships with colleagues who do not understand her reactions. Maria’s memory fragmentation also plays a significant role in exacerbating her symptoms. The disjointed nature of her memories can lead to confusion and anxiety. For example, she might start to recount the traumatic event but then lose track of the sequence of events, which causes her additional distress and reinforces her negative beliefs about herself and the world. The combination of these factors has created a self-reinforcing cycle that Maria struggles to break free from. Her triggers lead to intense physical reactions, fragmented memories, and heightened threat perceptions, all of which reinforce each other in a tightening loop. This cycle has significantly impacted her daily life, making it challenging for her to function effectively at work or maintain meaningful relationships. What finally brought Maria to seek help was the increasing isolation she felt and her growing fear that she would never regain control over her life. She is most afraid of feeling trapped by these symptoms but also hopes that with professional support, she can find a way to rebuild meaning in her life and manage her trauma more effectively.
